situations.scene: A heavy man in a good city overcoat steps off the noon train and asks Emil Ott for 'the doctor's sister', giving a married name. Ott glances along the platform at Ines before he answers.

The new engineer spreads a plan on the clinic counter: a cross-passage from the heading toward the old galleries, to drain them faster. 'You know the ground up there, Doctor, I'm told. Any objection?'

A woman Ines does not know brings in her eleven-year-old son with a grumbling pain low on the right. She mentions, in passing, that he tires on the stairs and goes a little blue about the lips when he runs.
At the bakery counter Otto Brandt says his wife's back is bad again and asks whether his daughter, now she is well, might go back to helping with the morning sifting.
A shot-firer from the new gang stops Ines on the portal road and shows her the brass lamp he has been issued. 'The flame never changes, Doctor, whatever the air's like. Is that good?'
Sanna, rushing before evening surgery, has the dispensary lamp lit on the high shelf and is topping it up from the oil jug without turning it down.
In the rebuilt bunkhouse the men have strung a line of wet socks and trousers a foot from the new stove's flue to dry them overnight. The flue collar is already scorched brown.
A girl from Tanner's Row brings word that the widow in the end house with the green door would like the doctor to look at a lump on her neck, if the doctor will come.

A letter from a solicitor in Graz: a small sum from the Calder estate lies unclaimed, and before he releases it he asks whether both daughters are content with how their mother's possessions were divided.
A navvy comes in on crutches, his left foot still bound. He says he was crushed at the face in October, and now the company's new clerk says he was off shift when it happened and will get nothing.
Frau Pichler at the post office hands over a letter with the city hospital's crest: the professor writes that the post is unexpectedly still open, and asks whether the doctor would reconsider.

The carter says nobody has paid him for the camp water carts in three weeks and he will stop on Monday. Up at the camp the men are grumbling that they could just pull the planks off the well by the spoil heap.
A constable from Grauberg calls: Voss's lawyer says the doctor bore the company a grudge over unpaid bills, and the constable wants to know whether that is so.
A clerk from the railway board writes that the tunnel will reopen to the heading next month, and asks whether the doctor would care to walk it with the district's new inspector beforehand.
Mira finds 'the ninth of March' marked on the kitchen calendar and asks, delighted, whether it is for her birthday party, and who is coming.
A letter from Dr. Brenner in the city: he proposes to write up 'the Kessel Pass outbreak' for a medical journal and asks whether Ines would put her name to it with his.
Sanna, pouring the morning coffee, asks whether the doctor wants her eggs boiled or fried today.
A small boy in the waiting room, swinging his legs while his mother is seen, asks Ines very seriously why snow is white when water isn't.
Wirth the postman, delivering a parcel of catalogues, complains that the wind has gone round to the north and asks whether she thinks it will snow before Sunday.
On the platform a traveller with a carpet bag asks Ines the time; the clock over the booking office has stopped at twenty past four.
